paragraphs: This page supports career exploration of routine testing, quality control, documentation, and anomaly handover. O*NET says practitioners may work under medical technologists' supervision; the occupational title does not establish independent diagnostic or report issuance authority.

Medical and clinical laboratory technicians turn patient specimens into reviewable test results: checking specimens against requests, processing and testing under procedures, analyzing results and identifying anomalies, performing quality controls and equipment maintenance, recording findings, and handing them over to authorized personnel. Work mainly takes place in controlled indoor laboratories, requires protective equipment and high accuracy, and involves specimens that may contain pathogens.

60-minute paper problem (editorially fictional, with no patients, specimens, or instrument operation): exercise rules require batch Q quality-control values to fall within 90—110 inclusive before paper checks may continue. Identifiers must match exactly. Any FLAG must be recorded and referred to the designated reviewer, never automatically ignored. Batch Q1 has quality-control value 108; Q2 has 112. Record A: Q1, request ID A01, specimen label A01, no FLAG. B: Q1, request B01, label B10, no FLAG. C: Q1, request C01, label C01, FLAG present. D: Q2, request D01, label D01, no FLAG. Classify each as ready for review, identity question pending confirmation, FLAG pending review, or batch quality-control failure pending handling, with reasons. Write a handover form and identify whose authorization still needs checking. The 90—110 interval is only a game rule, not a clinical quality-control or health reference range.

Reference solution: Q1's 108 meets the exercise interval; Q2's 112 exceeds the upper limit by 2. A is ready for review, which still does not authorize release of a real report. B has an identity question because B01≠B10; do not alter the label independently. Retain C's FLAG and refer it to the designated reviewer; this does not diagnose disease. D has a batch issue because Q2 fails; do not overwrite Q2 using Q1's passing value. For each record, retain the batch, original ID, original quality-control value, FLAG, judgment, unresolved questions, and handover recipient. Without authorized confirmation, do not write corrected or released. Spend 10 minutes reading rules, 25 minutes classifying independently, 15 minutes writing the handover, and 10 minutes comparing answers and retaining a corrected version.

This page covers O*NET 29-2012.00, Medical and Clinical Laboratory Technicians, referred to here as laboratory technicians: performing routine medical tests for disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, potentially under medical technologists' supervision. Common reported titles include Clinical Laboratory Technician, Laboratory Assistant, Laboratory Technician, Medical Laboratory Assistant, Medical Technician, Microbiology Technician, Specimen Processor, and Traveling Medical Laboratory Technician. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as Calibration Technologists and Technicians, Microbiologists, and Biological Technicians.

entries: Inputs: patient specimens (blood, body fluids, tissue), test requests and quality requirements, equipment such as analyzers and microscopes, reagents and quality-control materials, and infection-control and protective procedures.

Verifiable outputs: specimen checking and processing records, test and quality-control results, equipment maintenance and calibration records, anomaly review and escalation records, and traceable test reports.

Complete workflow: check specimens and requests → process and test under procedures → analyze results and identify anomalies → quality controls and equipment maintenance → review and record → retest anomalies and escalate, completing the loop.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether specimen identity and quality are adequate; whether methods and quality controls are in control; whether results match clinical information; whether anomalies require retesting or consultation with a pathologist; whether equipment calibration remains valid; and which release and diagnostic matters require authorized confirmation.

US O*NET respondents: 99% wear protective/safety equipment daily, 85% consider accuracy extremely important, 81% work in controlled indoor environments daily, 70% encounter disease or infection daily, and 57% consider consequences of error extremely serious. These percentages refer to different questions and response options, not infection probabilities, and do not establish Chinese hours or shift systems. Check shifts in specific job postings and contracts.

Research inputs: O*NET29-2012.00 identity, 14 tasks, RIC, and context concern technicians; wages, industries, and employment combine Clinical Laboratory Technologists and Technicians. 2025 wages and 2025—2035 projections; BLS OOH combined SOC29-2010 differs from O*NET's technician code. Do not extrapolate to Chinese qualifications or wages.

Verify first: specimen identity and condition, test requests and items, method and quality-control status, equipment calibration validity, infection-control and protective conditions, and anomaly and release judgments requiring authorized confirmation.

Work cycle: begin with checking specimens and requests, proceed through processing and testing, result analysis and anomaly identification, quality control and equipment maintenance, and end with review, documentation, and escalation. Do not test before specimen identity is confirmed, issue results before quality controls are in control, or proceed before anomaly or infection-control questions are confirmed.

Pathologists' official core function is diagnosing disease through examinations of organs, tissues, and body fluids. Technicians' routine testing and recording do not automatically confer physicians' diagnostic authority. Mainland China: professional technical personnel in medical institution clinical laboratories should have appropriate professional education and professional technical position qualifications. Reporting systems must distinguish operators from reviewers; diagnostic clinical laboratory reports are issued by licensed physicians, or by licensed assistant physicians in medical institutions in townships, ethnic townships, and towns (Administrative Measures, Articles 12 and 16—19). United States: CLIA sets laboratory quality and personnel requirements by testing complexity; nonwaived testing must meet applicable personnel standards. Separately check local licensure and organizational role authorization. O*NET's statement that practitioners may work under medical technologists' supervision is not a uniform supervision rule for all roles.
Difference from calibration technicians: calibration technicians focus on instrument calibration and measurement; this occupation focuses on routine patient specimen testing and result recording.

Microbiologists study microbial growth, structure, development, and other characteristics; this occupation centers on routine clinical testing. Roles may overlap, but similar names do not establish research or diagnostic qualifications.

Difference from biological technicians: biological technicians focus on laboratory research and preparation; this occupation focuses on clinical specimens and patient results, subject to infection-control and practice boundaries.

Pathologists diagnose disease through examinations of organs, tissues, and body fluids; this occupation performs routine tests and provides reviewable records. Medical report review and diagnostic authority require verification under the applicable jurisdiction and organization.
Tasks and AI: laboratory technicians' task exposure to AI does not equal job replacement. Humans remain responsible for specimen checks, result interpretation, and anomaly escalation.

Editorial trial hypothesis: use this page's fictional records to test AI-assisted table organization or handover drafts, checking original IDs, quality-control values, and FLAGs individually and recording omissions and unauthorized alterations. Do not use patient data or let AI diagnose or release results. Hot Technologies measures recruitment skill mentions; ILO provides a task-exposure method. Neither establishes this occupation's AI adoption rate, clinical performance, or replacement share.
Evidence method: task capability, organizational adoption, and employment outcomes are three different kinds of evidence and require separate verification.
Differences across directions: AI-related changes and remaining responsibilities differ across specimen testing, result review, equipment quality control, and handover.
Responsibility process: from checking inputs and limiting tasks to human review, documentation, and escalation.
Usage boundary: tool outputs must be traceable to original specimens, methods, quality-control states, and actual records.
Trial record organization using fictional inputs and check outputs field by field. This is an editorial hypothesis; organizational adoption and clinical performance have not been measured.
Authorized personnel review results, anomalies, and release judgments.

Not technicians separately, current vacancies, or an individual's hiring probability.

How to interpret these figures: explain employment levels, growth rates, net changes, and annual openings separately; they cannot be combined into an individual employment guarantee. Combined scope cannot replace a separately reported occupation. Organizational and regional differences are substantial; do not extrapolate across regions.
Fit signals: assess laboratory technician fit through observable behavior, without substituting personality labels for tasks, qualifications, and responsibility judgments.

Direct answer: if you can follow procedures for testing, documentation, and anomaly escalation under high accuracy and infection-control requirements, further exploration is worthwhile. Otherwise, compare adjacent directions first.
Positive signals: willingness to repeatedly check specimens and results, follow infection-control and quality-control procedures, and accept responsibility for test records.
Reasons for caution: if blood, body fluids, infection exposure, or highly repetitive checking cause marked discomfort, consider adjacent directions or nonclinical roles first.

Complete paper classification and handover of this page's four fictional records A—D, retaining initial answers and corrections. Do not perform real sampling, testing, or infection-control operations.

RIASEC (RIC): the interest code describes preferences for operating equipment and physical objects (Realistic), analytical reasoning (Investigative), and procedural data handling (Conventional). Use it only to generate hypotheses, not infer hiring or competence.

Big Five personality describes tendencies only. Observe in the work sample whether you preserve original B01/B10 values, avoid substituting 108 when quality control is 112, and retain C's FLAG under pressure. These observations cannot establish competence in a real role.
Labels such as MBTI cannot determine competence. First check actual tasks, standards, and responsibility boundaries, then decide whether to continue.

Specimen identity errors may affect patient safety. Check identifiers and requests under organizational procedures, preserve differences, and refer them to authorized personnel. Whether two-person checking is required depends on applicable procedures; this page does not present it as a uniform legal requirement for all roles.
Misinterpreted results or missed anomalies: failure to review results under quality-control and retesting rules may affect clinical decisions. Review under rules and escalate.

Infection exposure or inadequate protection: handling specimens without following infection-control and protective procedures may cause occupational exposure and infection. Wear protective equipment and handle waste under procedures.

Reporting despite equipment or quality-control anomalies may cause systematic errors. Record anomalies, investigate causes, correct, and review under the laboratory quality system. Authorized personnel decide whether testing and reporting may resume. This page provides no clinical operating instructions.

Common escalation rule: whenever specimens, results, equipment, or infection control raise questions, stop or isolate the relevant activity first. Submit facts, impacts, and unresolved questions to authorized personnel for confirmation before continuing.

Practical entry point: entry-level laboratory technician samples use only public or fictional data to demonstrate specimen checks, testing, and quality-control judgments. First confirm the role's first-year tasks and supervision arrangements.

US Job Zone 3 describes typical preparation through paths such as vocational training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree; not everyone must have all three. Specific education, personnel qualifications, and supervision depend on test types, state rules, and organizational roles. Mainland China: professional technical personnel in medical institution clinical laboratories should have appropriate professional education and professional technical position qualifications. Reporting systems must distinguish operators from reviewers; diagnostic clinical laboratory reports are issued by licensed physicians, or by licensed assistant physicians in medical institutions in townships, ethnic townships, and towns (Administrative Measures, Articles 12 and 16—19). United States: CLIA sets laboratory quality and personnel requirements by testing complexity; nonwaived testing must meet applicable personnel standards. Separately check local licensure and organizational role authorization. O*NET's statement that practitioners may work under medical technologists' supervision is not a uniform supervision rule for all roles.

Editorial portfolio: submit original A—D inputs, initial classifications, individual rationales, a handover form, comparison with the reference solution, and correction records. Paper work supports career exploration only and does not replace professional education, clinical training, qualifications, or real test-quality records.
Interviews and trials: demonstrate how you check specimens, handle anomalies under quality-control rules, follow infection control, and stop and escalate when anomalies occur.

Seven-day paper exploration, 30—60 minutes daily: Day 1, read this page's duties and jurisdictional boundaries. Day 2, draw a decision chart for identifiers, quality control, and FLAGs. Day 3, hide the reference and classify A—D. Day 4, write the handover and distinguish facts from unresolved questions. Day 5, compare with the reference and retain a corrected version. Day 6, ask a peer to challenge your reasons using only the problem statement. Day 7, compile work and feedback and write evidence for continuing, stopping, or changing direction. No sampling, testing, or patient data throughout. Peers are not qualification reviewers.

Certification directories only identify candidate paths. This page's list mixes laboratory technician, physician, and other professional credentials; not all entries can be described as applicable or required. First verify education, experience, and examination conditions with issuers, then state rules or Chinese job qualifications. The training page was not successfully read this round, so courses must not be invented from it.

Capability ladder: before entering laboratory technician work, verify the official occupational scope, actual employer requirements, education or training, local practice and supervision rules, and supervised tasks. Do not infer these directly from adjacent occupations. Advancement rests on reviewable testing and quality-control records, not a guaranteed number of years.

Transition path: before changing direction, list transferable skills in specimen processing, routine testing, quality control and equipment, documentation, and collaboration, alongside practice, method, and infection-control knowledge to acquire. Check each against adjacent roles' qualifications and responsibilities.

Transitioning toward calibration requires work-sample evidence of measurement science, standards applicability, ranges/errors, and calibration procedures, with target employer requirements checked separately. Clinical test records do not automatically equal metrological ability.
